query: I am investigating a quaternary equiatomic alloy with a face-centered cubic (FCC) structure, specifically looking for the relationship between its mechanical properties and its corrosion resistance. What hypotheses can be proposed regarding the plastic deformation mechanisms under uniaxial tension? Please provide supporting prior evidence for dislocation-based yielding, identify the boundary conditions where yield strength might become insensitive to strain rate, and propose a falsification experiment to distinguish between dislocation glide and phase transformation mechanisms.

generation.hypothesis: In quaternary equiatomic face-centered cubic (FCC) high-entropy alloys with high lattice distortion, the yield strength becomes insensitive to strain rate above a critical threshold (approx. 10^-2 s^-1) due to the saturation of thermally activated dislocation glide, where the dominant plastic deformation mechanism shifts from thermally activated dislocation glide to athermal glide driven by severe lattice friction, distinct from stress-induced phase transformation.
generation.material_initial_state: Quaternary equiatomic face-centered cubic (FCC) alloy with high configurational entropy and significant atomic size mismatch leading to high lattice distortion, similar to the CoCrFeMnNi prototype but with a specific quaternary composition.
generation.intervention: Apply uniaxial tensile loading at varying strain rates ranging from 10^-4 s^-1 to 10^0 s^-1 at room temperature.
generation.conditions: Room temperature (298 K), vacuum or inert atmosphere to prevent surface oxidation effects on bulk mechanical response, strain rates spanning 10^-4 to 10^0 s^-1.
generation.structural_mediator: High-density forest dislocations interacting with severe lattice distortion fields (solute atoms) creating a high Peierls barrier and high friction stress.
generation.mechanism: At low strain rates, dislocation motion is thermally activated over local energy barriers created by solute atoms. As strain rate increases, the thermal activation time becomes insufficient, and the stress required to move dislocations approaches the athermal limit (Peierls stress). Once the athermal limit is reached, further increases in strain rate do not significantly increase yield strength, causing the rate sensitivity to vanish. This behavior is characteristic of solid solution strengthening in FCC alloys and is distinct from phase transformation mechanisms which typically exhibit different strain-rate dependencies or hysteresis.
generation.predicted_outcome: A plot of yield strength vs. logarithmic strain rate will show a linear increase at low rates followed by a plateau (zero slope) at high rates. Post-deformation microscopy will reveal high dislocation densities and slip bands, but no evidence of new crystallographic phases (e.g., HCP or BCC) associated with deformation twinning or martensitic transformation.
generation.baseline: Standard dislocation glide theory for solid solution strengthened FCC alloys where yield strength typically scales with strain rate via a power law or logarithmic relationship until the athermal limit is reached, as observed in CoCrFeMnNi alloys [PMC8398136::chunk::001::introduction::d83bb5753a].
generation.boundary: The hypothesis holds for temperatures where thermal activation is significant at low rates but insufficient at high rates; it fails if the alloy has a stacking fault energy (SFE) low enough to induce stress-induced FCC-to-HCP phase transformation (martensitic transformation) or deformation twinning, which would introduce a distinct, non-linear strain rate dependence and microstructural changes not explained by dislocation saturation alone [PMC6093928::chunk::001::introduction::2dc33c3a9e].
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the exact critical strain rate threshold, which depends heavily on the specific elemental composition and the magnitude of the lattice distortion parameter. Additionally, if the alloy has a stacking fault energy (SFE) that is extremely low, deformation twinning might compete with or dominate dislocation glide, potentially altering the strain rate sensitivity profile.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction (XRD) and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) on identical samples of the quaternary alloy subjected to uniaxial tension at a strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1 (where the plateau is predicted) and 10^-1 s^-1. Compare the diffraction patterns and lattice imaging before and after yielding.
measurements: Lattice parameter shifts and peak broadening (indicative of dislocation density)
Appearance of new diffraction peaks corresponding to non-FCC phases (indicative of phase transformation)
Direct imaging of dislocation structures vs. twin boundaries or martensitic variants
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if new diffraction peaks corresponding to a different crystal structure (e.g., HCP or BCC) appear during deformation at the predicted plateau strain rates, or if the yield strength continues to increase linearly with strain rate beyond the predicted threshold without microstructural evidence of dislocation saturation.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are defined as equimolar or nonequimolar single- and multiphase solid solutions, depending on the number and type of principal/secondary metallic elements with the configurational entropy greater than 1.61 R , (where R is the gas constant) ( [1] , [2] ). The minimization of the Gibbs free energy by increasing the configurational entropy results in the formation of a single- or multiphase solid solution, such as body-centered cubic (BCC) ( [3] ), face-centered cubic (FCC) ( [4] ), and/or hexagonal close-packed solid-solution phases ( [5] ) instead of intermetallic compounds ( [6] ). Moreover, the random distribution of multiple elements with different atomic radii leads to a severely distorted lattice with variations in the interatomic distances along the crystallographic direction of the unit cells ( [3] ). These features, in turn, contribute to desirable mechanical properties, such as high hardness, strength, ductility, and softening resistance at room temperature (RT) and elevated temperatures ( [3] ).

This paper examines the microstructure and mechanical properties of Ta 20 Nb 20 Hf 20 Zr 20 Ti 20 . Two casting processes, namely, gravity casting and suction-assisted casting, were applied, both followed by Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP). The aim of the current study was to investigate the creep and tensile properties of the material, since the literature review revealed no data whatsoever regarding these properties. The main findings are that the HIP process is responsible for the appearance of a Hexagonal Close Packed (HCP) phase that is dispersed differently in these two castings. The HIP process also led to a considerable increase in the mechanical properties of both materials under compression, with values found to be higher than those reported in the literature. Contrary to the compression properties, both materials were found to be highly brittle under tension, either during room temperature tension tests or creep tests conducted at 282 °C. Fractography yielded brittle fracture without any evidence of plastic deformation prior to fracture.

High entropy alloys (HEAs) are a new class of metallic materials composed of multiple principle elements in equal or near-equal atomic proportions [1] , [2] . They have been receiving significant research interest owing to their exceptional mechanical and functional properties; see, e.g., refs [3] – [5] . Among various reported HEAs, the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi (Cantor alloy) [6] is a popular and important prototype of HEAs based on 3d transition metals. Within a wide range of temperature below its solidus, it usually forms a chemically disordered solid solution in face-centered cubic (fcc) structure at ambient pressure [6] – [9] . A unique mechanical characteristic of the Cantor alloy is an enhanced strength-ductility combination with decreasing temperature, while maintaining outstanding fracture toughness at cryogenic temperatures, which was demonstrated to be closely related to the formation of nano-twins and stacking faults in deformation [7] , [10] – [15] . Furthermore, due to the irreversible pressure-induced phase transition from the fcc to the hexagonal close-packed (hcp) lattice, the presence of the hcp structure was recently observed at ambient conditions [16] – [18] . Abstract The microstructure, temperature-dependent mechanical properties and deformation behaviors of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) additively manufactured by selective laser melting (SLM) were investigated. SLM-built HEA had a face-centered cubic (FCC) single-phase random solid solution. In addition, SLM-built HEA was composed of epitaxial growth grains, dislocation network and nano-sized oxides. Room- and high-temperature compression tests confirmed that SLM-built HEA has outstanding mechanical properties in all temperature ranges compared to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEAs reported up to the present. The excellent mechanical properties of SLM-built HEA were achieved with fine grains, high dislocation density and fine precipitates at low temperatures (25 °C to 600 °C), and by high dislocation density and fine precipitates at high temperatures (700 °C or higher). On the other hand, the deformation microstructure showed that slip and deformation twins are the main deformation mechanisms from 25 °C to 600 °C, and slip and partial recrystallization are the main deformation mechanisms above 700 °C. Nanomaterials are new age materials exhibiting exceptional mechanical, electronic, and optical properties due to their unique structure and high surface-area to volume ratio [ [1] ]. Among nanomaterials, one dimensional (1D) metallic nanowires (NWs) are widely used for different applications including nanoelectronics, optoelectronics, energy harvesting and storage, ultrasensitive sensing, and nanoelectromechanical devices [ [2] , [3] , [4] ]. At the nanoscale, 1D NWs usually exhibit ultra high strength, differently from bulk materials, which makes them ideal candidates for studying their fundamental deformation mechanisms. Dislocation nucleation from free surfaces and its subsequent propagation through NWs has been found to be a dominant deformation mechanism in metallic NWs such as Au, Ag, Cu, and Ni [ [5] , [6] , [7] , [8] , [9] , [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] ]. This enables reorientation to a more preferred phase, resulting in exceptional mechanical properties such as superplasticity, high yielding strength, pseudoelasticity, and shape memory effects [ [5] , [6] , [7] , [8] , [9] ].
